The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. [guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers
Baby 18 months, 11.7 kg, mother stopped breastfeeding at 4 months and gave Nan formula. Now baby has diarrhoea again and not growing well. Next boat to hospital is Friday, today is Tuesday. What to do now?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: BREAST FEEDING
---
Restart breastfeeding if mother still has some milk, it protects against diarrhoea and gives best nutrition. Even partial breastfeeding helps.
If no breast milk, give expressed milk from another mother or formula by cup not bottle, bottles hard to clean and cause more diarrhoea.
Check for danger signs now: unable to drink, vomits everything, lethargic, bloody stool, very thirsty with sunken eyes. If any, prepare for referral on Friday boat with pre-referral ORS.
If no danger signs, give extra fluids, continue feeding during diarrhoea, and return daily for weight check until Friday.
Teach mother solids from 6 months onward, no cow milk before 12 months, and breastfeeding should have continued longer.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES- INTRAVENOUS FLUIDS p65] When to give more - Babies usually do not need more fluids than the maintenance amount shown above, - Babies who are dehydrated, have ongoing losses (such as through a diarrhoea/vomiting) or spend a lot of time under phototherapy may need more fluid. It is important to closely monitor the baby (weigh baby daily) as it is easy to give them too much. When to give less - Very sick babies with respiratory distress or meningitis may need less fluid, as they can retain fluid. Check sodium levels and if low, restrict fluids to 2/3 maintenance. Which fluid? - Use 10% dextrose only, until day 2. DO NOT use this fluid after the first 3 days of life. o Top up 5% dextrose to make 10% dextrose o In 100ml burette, mix 90ml of 5% dextrose and 10ml of 50% dextrose - Babies older than 2 days need sodium and other electrolytes. o Use 5% dextrose and 0.9% saline or if not available 3% dextrose + 0.3% saline. o Always top up to make 10% dextrose - If the baby has low sodium, restrict the amount of fluid to 2/3 of maintenance and use Hartmann's or normal saline, topped up with glucose to make 10% o In 100ml paediatric burette, mix 80ml of Hartmann's and 20ml of 50% glucose - Some babies need more glucose, especially if they are very sick ...

assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: ASTHMA
---
Severe work of breathing with chest indrawing is a danger sign, but next boat tomorrow is the earliest transport.
Give Magnesium Sulfate 50% 0.9 ml IV (0.1 ml/kg = 50 mg/kg) over 20 minutes now if you can.
If not improving after MgSO4, give aminophylline 45 mg IV (5 mg/kg) slowly in burette over 1 hour.
If still very sick and no MgSO4 or aminophylline, give adrenaline 0.09 ml of 1:1000 SC/IV (0.01 ml/kg), repeat once in 15 minutes if no better.
Keep him propped up, watch for exhaustion or silent chest, and radio AHC now fo advice. Send on first boat tomorrow morning.

Baby born two days ago, birth weight around 2.0 kg. Mama says the baby is not feeding well and feels cold to touch. What should I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT
---
Keep the baby skin to skin with mama and cover the head, keep the room warm, no bath today.
Feed every 3 hours, day of life 2 for 2.0 kg means 15 ml each feed.
Check the baby can suck and is not floppy, and count the feeds written down each day.
Weigh the baby every day, good gain is 20 g a day or 100 to 150 g a week.
Come back at once if the baby stops feeding, feels cold, breathes fast, or goes yellow.

The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. [guideline: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE p64] Newborn deaths are concentrated towards the first three days of life, especially the first 24 hours. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. [guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

[guideline: SKIN DISEASES p96] IMPETIGO & CELLULITIS Painful blisters caused by staphylococcal or streptococcal skin infection SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Blisters and pustules rapidly spread and turn into irregular pussy sores with painful, shiny yellow weeping crusts. - May be associated with conditions any condition where the skin is broken including scabies, eczema, lice,, fungal infections, molluscum contagiosum and herpes simplex infection MANAGEMENT - Clean scabs away with antiseptic e.g. chlorhexidine. - Give cloxacillin 25mg/kg (max 500mg) orally every 6 hours for 7 to 10 days YAWS - Yaws are a contagious skin infection caused by Treponema pertenue - Infection is spread by direct skin-to-skin contact. The infection can remain in the body for a long time without causing any visible problems, or it can cause chronic sores and / or bone problems - Skin sores are typically o Raised and reddish brown, with a yellow crust. They may be ulcerated o Usually on the leg and painless o Unresponsive to standard sore treatments - Children with Yaws often develop bone problems, with pain in the long bones and swellings of the fingers, forearms, legs and bridge of the nose.The skin sore may have healed by this stage. - VDRL test is positive in Yaws o Children found to have a positive VDRL should be treated even if they don't currently have skin sores or bone problems - Give o benzathine penicillin IM as single dose - Child <20kg give 450mg (0.6 mega units) ...

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

Severe malnutrition with oedema of both feet and lethargy are danger signs. Baby must go to hospital now but road is flooded.
Call the AHC or hospital by radio or phone immediately. Ask for emergency transport advice or boat if possible.
While waiting: check malaria with RDT now. If positive or cannot test, this is not the guideline for treatment; the hospital will manage.
Keep baby warm, skin-to-skin with mama. Try to wake for feeds every 2-3 hours if she can suck; if not, do not force.
Do not give ACT or other medicines for malaria from your stock unless the hospital radio tells you to.
Write referral note: age 6 months, weight 6.6 kg, bilateral foot oedema, lethargic, poor breastfeeding attachment, weight loss 2 months, RDT result, no transport available, time of call.

8-year-old boy, 28.2 kg, in the clinic now. Had a long seizure at school. Head teacher brought him. I need to calculate phenytoin loading dose IV but I only have the 250 mg ampoules. How many ampoules and how to give safely?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Loading dose is 15-20 mg/kg: for 28.2 kg, give 423 mg to 564 mg.
Use two full ampoules (500 mg/10 mL) which is within safe range, or draw 8.5 mL for 425 mg.
For slow IV push: give 1-2 mg/kg/minute, so 28 to 56 mg/minute, taking about 8 to 15 minutes for 425 mg.
Maximum rate is 50 mg/minute, so do not push faster than that.
Flush with NS after at same slow rate, monitor breathing, and observe for another hour before sending home.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

[guideline: RHEUMATIC FEVER p90] Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) is a common cause of acquired childhood heart disease in Solomon Islands, most common in 5 - 14 year old children. The illness caused by a reaction to a bacterial infection (Group A streptococcus, GAS) which usually begins in the throat or potentially on the skin. ARF causes inflammation in joints and damage to the heart valves which can be permanent and is known as Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) If child is unwell and suspect ARF, refer to the nearest hospital for investigations and treatment. For further guidance please refer to the WHO Pocketbook of Hospital Care for children (2 nd Edition, 2013) and the Solomon Islands Protocol on Rheumatic Heart Disease

Always calculate on the amount of elemental iron in the mixture For Ferrous mixture 20mg/1ml (contains 6mg of elemental iron in 1ml): WEIGHT (kg) MIXTURE 3 - 5.9 6 - 9.9 10 - 14.9 15 - 19.9 20mg/ml 1ml 2.5ml 4ml 5ml - Plan to continue oral iron replacement for 3 months, recheck Hb o If no improvement, firstly check compliance with medication o Consider increasing dose o Consider alternative diagnosis (e.g chronic infection or disease) - If the child cannot take oral iron, consider IM injection. Discuss with paediatrician.
